The belief: once shared data lives in a

It's half true, and the true half is strong. Microsoft's docs call it a thread-safe dictionary and say you don't need locks of your own to add or remove items. Unlike a plain

, which needs your own synchronization for concurrent writes, it keeps its internal state consistent however many threads write at once. And most of the time, the code built on top of it looks correct in tests, where calls rarely overlap.
What the dictionary protects is its own state during each call. Your logic lives between the calls, and nothing protects that.

To avoid running unknown code while holding its internal lock, the dictionary calls the

If it calls an API, opens a connection or writes a log line, those side effects happen once per racing thread.
